name: Attendance Messages
title: Attendance Messages
answer: Attendance messages are brief, personalized communications to families that state a child's actual number of absences or what the child missed in class. They matter because parents often underestimate missed days, and correcting that misunderstanding can reduce chronic absence. The effect is modest at scale but real, and the teacher's personal detail is central.

sections.body: This idea addresses a gap between what schools know about attendance and what families believe. Many parents do not realize how many days their child has missed, so they may not see a problem that has already become chronic. Attendance messages close that gap by giving families the real total or a concrete example of missed learning. The approach solves a communication problem rather than a motivation problem, because the parent may simply be working from the wrong information. When the message is accurate and personal, it can prompt a change in behavior.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the early grades, the text describes postcards with a teacher's note about what the child missed, used with students in prekindergarten through second grade. A note that says the class learned the letter B today can mean more to a parent than a count of days. The text also describes mailings and personalized messages that tell parents the child's actual total absences, without tying them to a specific grade band. Districts can use their existing messaging platforms, and AI can help teachers draft notes quickly. The teacher then adds the personal detail, which keeps the message connected to the classroom.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, but it reports a series of randomized trials. In a trial with parents of more than 28,000 students at high risk of chronic absence, mailings that told parents their child's actual total absences cut chronic absence by 10 percent or more (Rogers & Feller, 2018). A trial in the early grades across 10 districts found a 15 percent reduction (Robinson et al., 2018). Six randomized trials run by districts themselves, covering about 78,000 students, found that personalized messages cut absences by about 1.9 percent (Berger et al., 2025); a trial across 47 rural districts found reductions of 1.7 to 4.5 percent at about four dollars per student (Swanson et al., 2026); and a trial using districts' existing messaging platforms at no added cost found reductions of 2 to 3 percent, though the neediest families were hardest to reach (Musaddiq et al., 2023). In a trial with more than 5,500 students in prekindergarten through second grade, postcards with a teacher's note about what the child had missed in class cut absences by 8.3 percent (Himmelsbach et al., 2021).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Effects at scale are smaller than the early trials, and the neediest families were hardest to reach when districts used existing messaging platforms. Personal touches matter, so a generic count of days may be less effective than a note about what the child missed. AI can assist with drafting notes quickly, while the teacher supplies the personal detail, and that decision stays with the teacher. The message must be accurate about the child's absences and connected to classroom learning, not a substitute for a human judgment about the family's situation.
